::: {#the-global-context-india-vs.-the-world .section .level3}
### The Global Context: India vs. The World

***Before dissecting India's internal vulnerabilities, we must establish
a macroeconomic baseline. Did India's tourism sector fare worse than the
global average during the 2020 border closures, and how did its recovery
trajectory compare?***

``` r
df_world <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-2001-2019-worldvsindia.csv")


colnames(df_world) <- c(
  "year", "world_millions", "world_pct_change", 
  "india_millions", "india_pct_change", "india_share_pct", "india_rank"
)

benchmark_data <- df_world %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    world_pct_change = as.numeric(world_pct_change),
    india_pct_change = as.numeric(india_pct_change)
  ) %>%
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2021) %>%
  select(year, world_pct_change, india_pct_change) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(world_pct_change, india_pct_change),
    names_to = "region",
    values_to = "growth_rate"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    region = ifelse(region == "world_pct_change", "Global Average", "India"),
    
    label_position = ifelse(region == "India", -1, 2) 
  )

ggplot(benchmark_data, aes(x = year, y = growth_rate, color = region, group = region)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(growth_rate, "%"), vjust = label_position), fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Global Average" = "#4575b4", "India" = "#d73027")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2021, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-85, 20)) +
  labs(
    title = "The Global Benchmark: Tourism Growth Rate (2015-2021)",
    subtitle = "Comparing India's crash and delayed recovery against the global tourism market",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Year-over-Year Growth Rate (%)",
    color = "Region"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray")
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***Results & Conclusion: The data reveals a complex two-part narrative.
In the initial 2020 crash, India actually proved marginally more
resilient than the global average, suffering a -64.8% contraction
compared to the catastrophic global contraction of -72.6%. This
temporarily inflated India's global market share to a record 1.58%.
However, the 2021 data highlights a severe delayed recovery. While the
rest of the world began to stabilize and post positive growth (+3.8%),
India's sector plunged a further -19.0%. This divergence perfectly maps
to the devastating internal Delta wave that struck India in the spring
of 2021, proving that domestic health crises extended the economic
damage long after global panic began to subside.***
:::

::: {#demographic-vulnerability-the-55-dependency .section .level3}
### Demographic Vulnerability: The 55+ Dependency

***Pandemics disproportionately threaten older demographics. We needed
to analyze if India's tourist base was uniquely exposed to this specific
health risk right before the border closures.***

``` r
df_age <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-2001-2019-agegroup.csv")
colnames(df_age) <- c(
  "year", "ftas_total", "age_0_14", "age_15_24", "age_25_34",
  "age_35_44", "age_45_54", "age_55_64", "age_65_plus", "not_reported"
)
plot_data_2019 <- df_age %>%
  filter(year == 2019) %>%
  select(age_0_14, age_15_24, age_25_34, age_35_44, age_45_54, age_55_64, age_65_plus) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "age_bracket", values_to = "percentage") %>%
  mutate(
    age_bracket = case_when(
      age_bracket == "age_0_14" ~ "0-14",
      age_bracket == "age_15_24" ~ "15-24",
      age_bracket == "age_25_34" ~ "25-34",
      age_bracket == "age_35_44" ~ "35-44",
      age_bracket == "age_45_54" ~ "45-54",
      age_bracket == "age_55_64" ~ "55-64",
      age_bracket == "age_65_plus" ~ "65+"
    ),
    risk_level = ifelse(age_bracket %in% c("55-64", "65+"), "High Risk (55+)", "Standard Risk")
  ) %>%
  mutate(age_bracket = factor(age_bracket, levels = c("0-14", "15-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65+")))

ggplot(plot_data_2019, aes(x = age_bracket, y = percentage, fill = risk_level)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), vjust = -0.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("High Risk (55+)" = "#d73027", "Standard Risk" = "#4575b4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-Pandemic Vulnerability: Age Profile of Tourists (2019)",
    subtitle = "Nearly 23% of inbound tourists were in the 55+ demographic",
    x = "Age Bracket",
    y = "Percentage of Total Arrivals (%)",
    fill = "COVID-19 Health Risk Level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***While the 2019 data above provides a clear anatomical breakdown of
the aging tourist base, a critical question remains for stakeholders:
Was 2019 an anomaly, or a permanent feature of the industry? The
following 5-year trend analysis answers this by proving this dependency
was a consistent structural flaw.***

``` r
high_risk_trend <- df_age %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2019) %>%
  mutate(percentage = age_55_64 + age_65_plus) 

ggplot(high_risk_trend, aes(x = year, y = percentage)) +
  geom_line(color = "#d73027", size = 1.5) +  
  geom_point(color = "#d73027", size = 4) +   
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), vjust = -1.5, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2019, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(20, 25)) + 
  labs(
    title = "The Persistent Vulnerability: High-Risk Tourists (2015-2019)",
    subtitle = "Isolating the 55+ demographic shows a clear, steady upward trend leading into the pandemic",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage of Total Arrivals (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank() 
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***The analysis proves that the reliance on older tourists was deeply
entrenched. Between 2015 and 2019, nearly 23% of all foreign arrivals
were consistently aged 55 and above. Because a quarter of the market
fell directly into the highest-risk medical category for COVID-19
complications, India's inbound tourism was highly susceptible to
health-related travel anxieties, compounding the damage of the eventual
border closures.***
:::

::: {#seasonal-vulnerability-the-winter-peak .section .level3}
### Seasonal Vulnerability: The Winter Peak

***Respiratory viruses, including COVID-19, historically surge during
colder winter months, prompting the strictest government lockdowns
globally. Did India's peak tourism season expose it to this specific
viral timeline?***

``` r
df_quarterly <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-2001-2019-quaterly.csv")

df_q_clean <- df_quarterly %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(
    year = 1,
    arrivals_total = 2,
    q1_pct = 3,
    q2_pct = 4,
    q3_pct = 5,
    q4_pct = 6
  )

plot_data_seasonal <- df_q_clean %>%
  filter(year == 2019) %>%
  select(q1_pct, q2_pct, q3_pct, q4_pct) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(), 
    names_to = "quarter", 
    values_to = "percentage"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    quarter_label = case_when(
      quarter == "q1_pct" ~ "Q1 (Jan-Mar)",
      quarter == "q2_pct" ~ "Q2 (Apr-Jun)",
      quarter == "q3_pct" ~ "Q3 (Jul-Sep)",
      quarter == "q4_pct" ~ "Q4 (Oct-Dec)"
    ),
    season_type = ifelse(quarter %in% c("q1_pct", "q4_pct"), "Peak Season (Winter)", "Off-Peak Season (Summer/Monsoon)")
  ) %>%
  mutate(quarter_label = factor(quarter_label, levels = c("Q1 (Jan-Mar)", "Q2 (Apr-Jun)", "Q3 (Jul-Sep)", "Q4 (Oct-Dec)")))

ggplot(plot_data_seasonal, aes(x = quarter_label, y = percentage, fill = season_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), vjust = -1, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Peak Season (Winter)" = "#d95f02", "Off-Peak Season (Summer/Monsoon)" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 35)) + # Give room for the text labels
  labs(
    title = "Pre-Pandemic Seasonal Vulnerability (2019)",
    subtitle = "59% of India's tourism relies on Q1 and Q4, exposing the sector to winter-driven COVID-19 waves",
    x = "Quarter",
    y = "Percentage of Annual Arrivals (%)",
    fill = "Season Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray")
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***To prove that this massive winter dependency wasn't just a
single-year fluke driven by specific events in 2019, we must expand the
scope to a 5-year historical view. As the trend below demonstrates, the
industry's reliance on the viral-prone Q1 and Q4 quarters was a systemic
vulnerability.***

``` r
colnames(df_quarterly) <- c(
  "year", "arrivals_total", "q1_pct", "q2_pct", "q3_pct", "q4_pct"
)
breakdown_data <- df_quarterly %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2019) %>%
  select(year, q1_pct, q4_pct) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(q1_pct, q4_pct),
    names_to = "specific_quarter",
    values_to = "percentage"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    
    specific_quarter = case_when(
      specific_quarter == "q1_pct" ~ "Q1 (Jan-Mar)",
      specific_quarter == "q4_pct" ~ "Q4 (Oct-Dec)"
    ),
    specific_quarter = factor(specific_quarter, levels = c("Q4 (Oct-Dec)", "Q1 (Jan-Mar)"))
  )

totals_data <- df_quarterly %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) %>%
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2019) %>%
  mutate(total_peak_pct = q1_pct + q4_pct)

ggplot(breakdown_data, aes(x = year, y = percentage, fill = specific_quarter)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5, color = "black") +
  
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  
  geom_text(
    data = totals_data,
    aes(x = year, y = total_peak_pct, label = paste0("Total Peak: ", total_peak_pct, "%"), fill = NULL),
    vjust = -1.2, fontface = "bold", size = 3, color = "#005a32"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Q1 (Jan-Mar)" = "#41ab5d", "Q4 (Oct-Dec)" = "#006d2c")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2019, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 68)) + 
  labs(
    title = "The Seasonal Vulnerability: Peak Winter Arrivals (2015-2019)",
    subtitle = "Showing the consistent 58-59% reliance on winter travel, exposing the sector to virus seasonality",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage of Total Arrivals (%)",
    fill = "Peak Season Quarters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank() 
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***The data shows a massive, unyielding seasonal concentration.
Consistently over the 5-year pre-pandemic baseline, nearly 60% of
India's annual tourism occurred in just two quarters: Q1 (Jan-Mar) and
Q4 (Oct-Dec). Because India's tourism lifecycle is deeply reliant on the
winter months, the sector possessed a built-in vulnerability to the
seasonality of global viral outbreaks. When the initial global lockdowns
took effect in late March 2020, the timing flawlessly eradicated India's
most economically vital quarters.***
:::

::: {#elasticity-of-travel-purpose-of-visit .section .level3}
### Elasticity of Travel: Purpose of Visit

***In tourism economics, "essential" travel (such as medical procedures
or diaspora returning for family emergencies) is rigid and resilient.
"Discretionary" travel (leisure and vacations) is highly elastic and is
the first expense canceled during a crisis.***

``` r
df_reason <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-2019_region-and-reason.csv")

colnames(df_reason) <- c(
  "region", "country", "total_arrivals", "business_pct", 
  "leisure_pct", "medical_pct", "diaspora_pct", "others_pct"
)

purpose_data <- df_reason %>%
  filter(country == "Grand Total") %>%
  select(business_pct, leisure_pct, medical_pct, diaspora_pct, others_pct) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(), 
    names_to = "purpose", 
    values_to = "percentage"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    purpose = case_when(
      purpose == "leisure_pct" ~ "Leisure & Holiday",
      purpose == "business_pct" ~ "Business & Professional",
      purpose == "diaspora_pct" ~ "Indian Diaspora (VFR)",
      purpose == "medical_pct" ~ "Medical Tourism",
      purpose == "others_pct" ~ "Others"
    ),
    vulnerability_level = ifelse(purpose == "Leisure & Holiday", "Highly Discretionary (High Flight Risk)", "More Rigid/Essential")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(percentage)) %>%
  mutate(purpose = factor(purpose, levels = purpose))

ggplot(purpose_data, aes(x = purpose, y = percentage, fill = vulnerability_level)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")), vjust = -0.8, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Highly Discretionary (High Flight Risk)" = "#d73027", "More Rigid/Essential" = "#4575b4")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 68)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Purpose Vulnerability: Why Tourists Visited India (2019)",
    subtitle = "Over 57% of all arrivals were purely discretionary leisure travelers,\nleaving the sector highly exposed to global panic",
    
    x = "Stated Purpose of Visit",
    y = "Percentage of Total Arrivals (%)",
    fill = "Travel Elasticity"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1, size = 7, face = "bold"),
    
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 15, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15)
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***Looking at the 2019 pre-pandemic baseline, an overwhelming 57.1% of
all arrivals to India were purely discretionary "Leisure, Holiday &
Recreation" travelers. Conversely, more rigid travel categories like
Business (14.7%), Diaspora/VFR (12.7%), and Medical (6.4%) made up a
distinct minority. This highlights a severe "Purpose Vulnerability." The
sector was built almost entirely on non-essential travel, leaving it
with virtually no economic buffer or essential travel baseline to fall
back on when the global panic began.***
:::

::: {#geographic-concentration-the-hub-wipeout .section .level3}
### Geographic Concentration: The Hub Wipeout

***A national percentage drop doesn't show the true economic damage. We
need to analyze where the highest volume of tourists vanished from.***

``` r
df_states <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-statewise_2019-2020_domestic_foreign.csv")

colnames(df_states) <- c(
  "s_no", "state_name", "domestic_2019", "foreign_2019", 
  "domestic_2020", "foreign_2020", "growth_domestic_pct", "growth_foreign_pct"
)
hub_data <- df_states %>%
  filter(!grepl("Total", state_name, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    foreign_2019 = as.numeric(foreign_2019),
    foreign_2020 = as.numeric(foreign_2020)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(foreign_2019)) %>%
  slice(1:5) %>%
  select(state_name, foreign_2019, foreign_2020) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(foreign_2019, foreign_2020),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "tourist_volume"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    
    year = ifelse(year == "foreign_2019", "2019 (Pre-Pandemic Peak)", "2020 (Pandemic Collapse)"),
    
    label_text = paste0(round(tourist_volume / 1000000, 1), "M"),
    
    state_name = factor(state_name, levels = unique(state_name))
  )


ggplot(hub_data, aes(x = state_name, y = tourist_volume, fill = year)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label_text), 
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), 
    vjust = -0.5, 
    fontface = "bold", 
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("2019 (Pre-Pandemic Peak)" = "#4575b4", "2020 (Pandemic Collapse)" = "#d73027")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"), limits = c(0, 8000000)) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Geographic Concentration: The Collapse of India's Top 5 Hubs",
    subtitle = "These 5 states handled ~70% of all international tourists in 2019. The border closures \nwiped out millions of visitors overnight, causing highly concentrated economic damage.",
    x = "State / Union Territory",
    y = "Foreign Tourist Visits (in Millions)",
    fill = "Timeline"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 15, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15)
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***India's international tourism market was highly centralized. Out of
all states and union territories, just five hub states (Tamil Nadu,
Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, and West Bengal) processed nearly 70%
of the entire country's foreign arrivals in 2019. Consequently, the
COVID-19 travel freeze did not spread economic damage evenly across the
subcontinent. It acted as a highly targeted economic strike, wiping out
millions of visitors and billions in revenue within these five specific
state economies overnight.***
:::

::: {#the-ground-reality-micro-impact-at-top-monuments .section .level3}
### The Ground Reality: Micro-Impact at Top Monuments

***Finally, we look at the gates of India's most famous sites to see the
true micro-economic impact and whether domestic tourism provided a
safety net.***

``` r
df_monuments <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\gagan\\OneDrive\\Desktop\\Group 18 DARP\\India-Tourism-Statistics-2021-monuments.csv")
colnames(df_monuments) <- c(
  "circle", "monument_name", "domestic_19_20", "foreign_19_20", 
  "domestic_20_21", "foreign_20_21", "growth_domestic_pct", "growth_foreign_pct"
)
top_monuments <- df_monuments %>%
  filter(!grepl("Total", monument_name, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    foreign_19_20 = as.numeric(foreign_19_20),
    growth_domestic_pct = as.numeric(growth_domestic_pct),
    growth_foreign_pct = as.numeric(growth_foreign_pct)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(foreign_19_20)) %>%
  slice(1:5) %>%
  select(monument_name, growth_domestic_pct, growth_foreign_pct) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(growth_domestic_pct, growth_foreign_pct),
    names_to = "tourist_type",
    values_to = "crash_percentage"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    tourist_type = ifelse(tourist_type == "growth_domestic_pct", "Domestic Collapse", "Foreign Collapse"),
    monument_name = str_wrap(monument_name, width = 12),
    
    monument_name = factor(monument_name, levels = unique(monument_name))
  )
ggplot(top_monuments, aes(x = monument_name, y = crash_percentage, fill = tourist_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), color = "black", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(crash_percentage, "%")), 
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), 
    vjust = 1.5, 
    fontface = "bold", 
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Foreign Collapse" = "#d73027", "Domestic Collapse" = "#fdae61")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-105, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = "The Ground Reality: Footfall Crash at Top Monuments (2020-21)",
    subtitle = "While foreign footfall was almost totally annihilated (~99% drop),\ndomestic travel provided a partial safety cushion",
    
    x = "Monument",
    y = "Percentage Drop in Footfall (%)",
    fill = "Market Segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f8f9fa", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff", color = "lightgray"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 15, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15)
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,){role="img"
aria-label="" width="672"}

***Isolating the top 5 most internationally visited monuments reveals a
bifurcated market. Foreign foot traffic did not just decline; it was
almost entirely eradicated, posting devastating drops of roughly 98% to
99% across the board. However, the data highlights the immense power of
the "Domestic Cushion." Despite a massive \~70% drop in domestic travel,
India's sheer population scale meant that sites like the Taj Mahal still
processed over 1.2 million local visitors during the 2020-21 pandemic
window. While the lucrative international market was wiped out, the
massive internal domestic market acted as a critical economic
life-support system for local monument economies.***
:::
:::
